topics.title: Houthi Rebels Capture Strategic Port City Mokha in Yemen

subtopics.title: Capture of Mokha and Red Sea stakes
subtopics.summary: Iran-backed Houthi forces seized the Red Sea port city of Mokha in Taiz Governorate, along with Perim and Zuqar islands. Mokha lies about 80 km from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, so Houthi control of the area threatens shipping routes between Asia and Europe. Government forces withdrew south towards Dhubab, while Houthi forces advanced towards the Hanish Islands.
facts: Houthis, an Iran-backed group, seized Mokha port city in Taiz Governorate.
Houthis also seized Perim and Zuqar Islands in Yemen.
Mokha is located about 80 km from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Bab el-Mandeb Strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
After Mokha fell, government forces moved south towards Dhubab.
Houthi forces advanced towards the Hanish Islands in the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia shut its East-West Oil Pipeline after drone strikes from Iraq.
Earlier Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping forced some vessels onto longer routes around Africa.
Renewed fighting caused civilian displacement and disrupted local supply lines.

subtopics.title: Houthi movement: identity and rise
subtopics.summary: The Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, are mainly Zaidi Shia Muslims and members of the Houthi tribe, and they oppose Israel and the US. Their founder, Hussein al-Houthi, was killed by Yemeni forces in Saada in 2004, which sparked the Houthi insurgency and the Saada Wars. The Houthis later seized Saada and captured Sanaa in 2014, forcing President Hadi to flee abroad in 2015.
facts: The Houthi movement is officially known as Ansar Allah (Supporters of God).
Houthis are primarily composed of Zaidi Shia Muslims and members of the Houthi tribe.
Founder: Zaidi religious leader Hussein al-Houthi; current leader: Abdul-Malik al-Houthi.
Houthis began as an opposition movement to President Ali Abdullah Saleh in the 2000s.
Founder was killed by Yemeni forces in Saada in 2004, sparking the Houthi insurgency.
Saada Wars ran from 2004 to 2010.
The 2011 Yemen Uprising forced Saleh to transfer power to his deputy, Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi.
Houthis seized Saada and captured Sanaa in 2014, forcing Hadi to flee abroad in 2015.
Houthis claimed responsibility for a missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport in 2017.
Houthis ideology: opposition to Israel and the US; part of the Iranian-led Axis of Resistance.

subtopics.title: Civil war and the 2018 peace deals
subtopics.summary: After the Houthi takeover of Sanaa, Saudi Arabia intervened militarily from 2015 to restore the internationally recognised government. The Stockholm Agreement, reached in Sweden on 13 December 2018, has three main components and was endorsed by the UN Security Council under resolution 2451. The Hodeidah ceasefire, effective from midnight on 17 December 2018, required the Houthis to withdraw from the ports and Hodeidah City under UN-chaired supervision.
facts: The Saudi-led intervention began in 2015 to reinstate the internationally recognised government.
The Stockholm Agreement was agreed in Sweden on 13 December 2018 at UN-mediated talks.
The Stockholm Agreement has three main components: Hudaydah Agreement, Prisoner Exchange Agreement and Taiz Agreement.
The UN Security Council endorsed the Stockholm Agreement under resolution 2451 (2018).
The Hodeidah ceasefire took effect from midnight on 17 December 2018.
The ceasefire covered Hodeidah City and the ports of Hodeidah, Ras Isa and Saleef.
Under the agreement, the Houthis withdraw from the ports and from Hodeidah City.
A UN-chaired committee including both sides oversees the withdrawal of forces.
Yemeni ports fall under local forces, who send port revenues to the country's central bank.

subtopics.title: North-South divide and southern separatism
subtopics.summary: Yemen existed as two separate states until 1990, when the North and South merged under Ali Abdullah Saleh. Power stayed heavily centralised after unification, which fuelled southern resentment and led to an attempted secession and brief civil conflict in 1994. The Southern Movement (Al-Hirak) formed in 2007, and the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council now seeks autonomy or independence for the south.
facts: Until 1990, Yemen existed as two countries: the Yemen Arab Republic (North) and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen (South).
North Yemen was supported by the US and Saudi Arabia; South Yemen was backed by the Soviet Union.
In 1990 the two states merged to form the Republic of Yemen.
Ali Abdullah Saleh had governed North Yemen since 1978 and became President of the unified state.
Centralised power after unification created resentment in the south.
By 1994 southern leaders attempted secession, leading to a brief civil conflict.
The Southern Movement (Al-Hirak) formed in 2007 and demands greater autonomy or independence.
The Southern Transitional Council is backed by the UAE and has expanded influence in Hadramout and Mahra.
A pro-government military bloc opposes the STC's separatist agenda and receives backing from Saudi Arabia.

subtopics.title: Mukalla strike and UAE troop withdrawal
subtopics.summary: In January 2026, Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes on Mukalla Port in southern Yemen after a consignment from Fujairah in the UAE arrived there, which Riyadh alleged contained arms for separatist groups. The UAE rejected the allegation, saying the vehicles were meant exclusively for its own forces. The UAE then pulled its troops out, citing security risks, a counter-terrorism-only mandate and the view that Yemen's future should be decided by Yemenis.
facts: Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes on Mukalla Port in southern Yemen.
The strike followed the arrival of a consignment from Fujairah (UAE).
Riyadh alleged the consignment contained arms meant for southern separatist groups.
The UAE said the shipment consisted of vehicles meant exclusively for UAE forces.
The UAE termed the claims of an arms transfer to separatists unfounded.
The UAE pulled troops out in January 2026 following the Mukalla airstrikes.
Security concern: escalating airstrikes raised risks to UAE personnel in the region.
Limited mandate: the UAE's military presence in Yemen is confined to counter-terrorism operations.
Political messaging: Yemen's future political structure should be determined by Yemenis themselves.

topics.title: Indus Waters Treaty and India's rejection of the Hague ruling

subtopics.title: Treaty basics and river allocation
subtopics.summary: The Indus Waters Treaty, 1960, is a bilateral water-sharing agreement between India and Pakistan that was facilitated by the World Bank. It allocates the Eastern rivers to India and the Western rivers primarily to Pakistan. India keeps limited, conditional rights on the Western rivers, including run-of-river power generation.
facts: Signed on 19 September 1960, after eight years of negotiations
Bilateral water-sharing agreement between India and Pakistan
Facilitated by the World Bank
Eastern rivers: Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, with exclusive and unrestricted use for India
Western rivers: Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, allocated primarily to Pakistan
India's rights on Western rivers are limited and subject to treaty conditions
Permitted uses on Western rivers include domestic use, limited agricultural use and run-of-river hydroelectric generation
India can build run-of-river hydro projects with minimum storage for conservation and flood management

subtopics.title: Three-tier dispute-resolution mechanism
subtopics.summary: The treaty provides a three-tiered route for disputes, starting with the Permanent Indus Commission for bilateral discussion. Technical differences that the Commission cannot resolve may go to a Neutral Expert, while formal legal disputes may be referred to a Court of Arbitration. The Court of Arbitration is constituted under Annexure G of the treaty.
facts: The treaty provides a three-tiered dispute mechanism
Permanent Indus Commission is the first institutional mechanism and provides a forum for bilateral discussion and information exchange
The Permanent Indus Commission meets at least once a year
Neutral Expert handles technical differences the Commission cannot resolve
The Neutral Expert is appointed through a mechanism involving the World Bank
The Neutral Expert route primarily addresses technical questions
Court of Arbitration handles formal legal disputes referred under the treaty
The Court of Arbitration is constituted under Annexure G and consists of 5 members

subtopics.title: Court of Arbitration's findings
subtopics.summary: The Court of Arbitration held that the treaty continues to apply and that India's decision to place it in abeyance was not permissible. It said the treaty does not deal with terrorism or use of force, so cross-border terrorism was not accepted as a material breach. The tribunal also imposed interim limits on construction at the Ratle project.
facts: The treaty continues in force until terminated by a duly ratified treaty (Article XII(4))
Article III(1) obliges India to let flow the waters of the Western rivers to Pakistan
Placing the treaty in abeyance was held not permissible under the treaty or international law
The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 was applied in the ruling
The treaty does not provide India a unilateral mechanism to suspend obligations
The treaty contains no provisions on terrorism or use of force
Interim limits bar concreting of specified parts of the Ratle dam wall and power intake beyond prescribed levels
The Ratle restrictions last until 90 days after the Neutral Expert's final determination

subtopics.title: India's objection to the tribunal
subtopics.summary: India rejects the ruling, saying the tribunal was constituted by the World Bank contrary to the treaty and has no jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions. India argues the treaty sets a graded, sequential route that ends with a court only after the Neutral Expert step. Pakistan and India initiated parallel proceedings in 2016, and the World Bank paused and later resumed the two processes.
facts: India has rejected the ruling and has neither recognised the tribunal's legitimacy nor participated in its proceedings
India's Ministry of External Affairs says the Court of Arbitration was constituted by the World Bank contrary to the treaty
India's abeyance decision after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack remains valid according to New Delhi
India says the tribunal has no jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions or infrastructure projects on the western rivers
India's position: question, then Permanent Indus Commission, then Neutral Expert, then legal dispute or Court of Arbitration
In 2016, Pakistan initiated proceedings seeking a Court of Arbitration
In 2016, India requested appointment of a Neutral Expert to examine technical aspects
In 2016, the World Bank paused both the arbitration and Neutral Expert processes
In 2022, the World Bank allowed both processes to move forward
India took part in Neutral Expert proceedings but not in Court of Arbitration proceedings

subtopics.title: Indus river system and water-sharing principles
subtopics.summary: The Indus is a trans-boundary river and the longest river in Pakistan, and its main tributaries have distinct sources in Tibet, Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh. The booklet lists three international instruments on shared water: the Helsinki Rules of 1966, the Helsinki Convention of 1992 and the UN Watercourses Convention of 1997. India, China and Pakistan have not signed the UN Watercourses Convention.
facts: The Indus is a trans-boundary river and the longest river in Pakistan
The Indus originates at the Bokhar Chu Glacier near Mt Kailash, Mansarovar, Tibet
The Jhelum rises at the Verinag Spring in the Kashmir Valley and joins the Chenab at Trimmu
The Chenab originates near Bara Lacha Pass in Lahul-Spiti (HP) and joins the Satluj at Panchnad
The Ravi rises in the Kullu Hills near Rohtang Pass and joins the Chenab a little above Rangpur
The Beas originates near Rohtang Pass and joins the Satluj at Harike
The Satluj rises from the Manasarovar-Rakas Lakes in Tibet and joins the Indus a little above Mithankot
Helsinki Rules 1966 were adopted by the International Law Association to regulate water use in an international drainage basin
Helsinki Convention 1992 provides a framework for preventing and controlling water pollution across national borders
UN Watercourses Convention 1997 codified law on non-navigational uses of international watercourses; India, China and Pakistan have not signed it

topics.title: Cardiff Pact and UK Federal Challenge

subtopics.title: Devolution and the asymmetric UK framework
subtopics.summary: Devolution transfers powers from the central government to subnational institutions, while the centre keeps ultimate constitutional authority. In the UK, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved institutions, but the extent and nature of their powers differ, so the arrangement is asymmetric rather than uniform. The UK Treasury uses the Barnett Formula to set changes in block grant funding for these administrations.
facts: Devolution means transfer of powers from central government to subnational institutions
Ultimate constitutional authority is retained at the centre
Devolved institutions in the UK: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
Extent and nature of devolved powers differ among the three
UK devolution is asymmetric rather than uniform
Scotland Act 1998 established the Scottish Parliament and devolved substantial domestic powers
Government of Wales Act 1998 established the Welsh Legislature, now known as the Senedd
Barnett Formula is used by the UK Treasury to set block grant changes
UK Internal Market Act 2020 regulates the domestic UK market after Brexit
Devolved governments criticised the 2020 Act as reducing their regulatory autonomy

subtopics.title: Historical formation of the Union
subtopics.summary: The UK's constituent nations joined the union at different points. Wales was incorporated into the English legal and political system through the Act of Union of 1536, while later Acts of Union brought Scotland (1707) and Ireland (1801) into the state. After most of Ireland became independent in 1922, six counties remained within the UK as Northern Ireland.
facts: Wales was incorporated into the English legal and political system; Act of Union in 1536
Acts of Union, 1707 united the English and Scottish Parliaments into the Kingdom of Great Britain
Act of Union, 1801 brought Ireland into the United Kingdom
Anglo-Irish War (1919-21) preceded Irish independence
In 1922 most of Ireland became independent
Six counties formed Northern Ireland within the UK
The state is now the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

subtopics.title: Good Friday Agreement and Northern Ireland
subtopics.summary: The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement, signed on 10 April 1998, ended the conflict known as The Troubles in Northern Ireland. It set up power-sharing government, allowed reunification with Ireland subject to a referendum, and let citizens hold Irish or British nationality or both. After the 2022 deadlock over government formation, a new deal was published as the command paper Safeguarding the Union.
facts: Signed on 10 April 1998 at Belfast; ended a 30-year-old civil war known as The Troubles
Power-sharing government formed on the wishes of Republicans and Unionists, who share governance equally
People can seek reunification with Ireland at any time, subject to a referendum
Citizens can hold Irish or British nationality or both
Agreement abolished border checks and encouraged freedom of movement across UK and Ireland
A border poll on Irish reunification can be called by the UK Secretary of State for Northern Ireland when conditions show majority support
After Brexit, Northern Ireland shared a land border with the Republic of Ireland, an EU member
Border checks between Great Britain and Northern Ireland angered Unionists
The DUP leader refused to allow government formation after the May 2022 Northern Ireland polls
A new deal was published as a command paper called Safeguarding the Union

subtopics.title: Cardiff Pact and the UK federal challenge
subtopics.summary: The Cardiff Pact is a political Memorandum of Understanding signed in Cardiff by leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and it is not a legally binding treaty. It asks Westminster to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change and affirms each nation's right to hold independence referendums. The UK government rejects new referendums, relying on a 2022 Supreme Court ruling that the Scottish Parliament cannot legislate for one without Westminster's consent.
facts: Cardiff Pact is an inter-party accord signed in Cardiff (Wales)
Signatories include John Swinney (SNP), Rhun ap Iorwerth (Plaid Cymru) and Michelle O'Neill (Sinn Fein Vice President)
Mary Lou McDonald (Sinn Fein President) also attended
The pact is a political Memorandum of Understanding, not a legally binding treaty
Core objectives: prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change; affirm right to hold independence referendums; coordinate policies on economy, energy and European relations
Scotland and Wales would seek EU membership as new states
Northern Ireland would rejoin the EU through unification with the Republic of Ireland
All three devolved administrations are now led by pro-independence parties
UK government rejects new independence referendums without appropriate constitutional and legal authority
2022 UK Supreme Court ruling (Reference by the Lord Advocate): Scottish Parliament cannot unilaterally legislate for an independence referendum without Westminster's consent

topics.title: Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act 2026

subtopics.title: Passage and timeline
subtopics.summary: The United States enacted the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 after House passage and Senate approval. The House voted 262 to 159 on 16 September, and the President signed the Act into law on 18 September 2026. The measure matters for India because India remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude.
facts: House of Representatives passed the legislation 262-159 on 16 Sep
The legislation followed Senate approval
Presidential signing into law on 18 Sep 2026
Act aims primarily at increasing economic pressure on Russia over the Ukraine War
Act also extends and strengthens certain sanctions against Iran
India is significant because it remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude

subtopics.title: Key provisions
subtopics.summary: The Act authorises tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, a substantial reduction from the 500% original proposal. It also authorises tariffs of up to 500% on Russian-origin goods, subject to specified exceptions. A 180-day review cycle for relevant purchasers and defined conditions for ending the sanctions framework complete its core design.
facts: Tariffs of up to 100% on the 5 largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas
100% ceiling is a substantial reduction from the original 500% proposal
Tariffs also target the Top 5 facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion
USTR reassesses relevant purchasers under a 180-day review cycle
Tariffs of up to 500% on Russian-origin goods, subject to specified exceptions
Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 is extended through 2031
Gas exception: importing less than 15% of natural gas from Russia and taking significant steps to reduce such imports
Framework may be affected if Russia signs an accepted peace agreement, ceases military hostilities and ends activities undermining the Ukrainian Government

subtopics.title: Legal permanence and US trade tools
subtopics.summary: The earlier 25% punitive tariff on India was based on an Executive Order, and in February 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the broader tariff regime that included it. The new measure has been passed by Congress, signed and converted into federal law, which gives it greater legal permanence. A presidential waiver under the Act requires formal justification to Congress.
facts: Earlier 25% punitive tariff on India was based on an Executive Order
In February 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the broader tariff regime
New measure was passed by Congress, signed and converted into federal law
Federal law gives the new measure greater legal permanence than an executive tariff
Presidential waiver requires formal justification to Congress
Section 301 of the Trade Act, 1974 lets the USTR investigate foreign trade practices
Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, 1962 restricts imports seen as a threat to national security
United States imposed tariffs of 50% on steel, aluminium, copper and certain related products
India faces a 10% tariff linked to a U.S. investigation into goods produced using forced labour

subtopics.title: Global and India implications
subtopics.summary: The measure illustrates growing use of secondary sanctions and tariff instruments to influence the behaviour of third countries. It could change global oil trade patterns as major buyers diversify suppliers and reconfigure energy contracts. For India, Russia is the top oil supplier, so potential tariffs complicate bilateral trade while India balances strategic autonomy with its energy interests.
facts: Measure illustrates growing use of secondary sanctions and tariff instruments
Major buyers may diversify suppliers and reconfigure energy contracts
Buyers may increase purchases before potential tariff measures
Buyers may develop alternative payment and logistics arrangements
Russia is India's top oil supplier
Potential tariffs complicate India-U.S. bilateral trade and economic ties
Higher import bills drive up transport, logistics, manufacturing and consumer prices
Discounted crude improves economics, though replacing large volumes is logistically challenging
Balancing relationships with major powers while protecting national energy interests

topics.title: India Rejects Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission

subtopics.title: Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission
subtopics.summary: Pakistan and China have set up a Boundary Joint Commission that traces back to their 2013 boundary management agreement and was operationalised in September 2026. India rejects the body because it treats the territory involved as its own and does not recognise the 1963 agreement under which Shaksgam Valley passed to China. The Commission sits alongside China-Pakistan connectivity links such as the Khunjerab crossing and CPEC, which India opposes.
facts: Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission was operationalised in Sep 2026; inaugural meeting held in Islamabad.
The Commission originates from the 2013 Pakistan-China Agreement on Boundary Management System.
Article 45 of the 2013 agreement provides for a Joint Commission to supervise implementation of border management arrangements.
Commission is intended to facilitate coordination on border management, joint surveys, trade flows and people-to-people connectivity.
1963 China-Pakistan Boundary Agreement was signed on 2 March 1963.
Under the 1963 agreement, Pakistan transferred approx 5,180 sq km of Shaksgam Valley (Trans-Karakoram Tract) to China.
India has never recognised the 1963 Sino-Pakistan Boundary Agreement and considers it illegal and invalid.
India argues Pakistan has no locus standi over territory India regards as under Pakistan's illegal occupation.
Khunjerab Crossing/Corridor is the principal overland connection between China and Pakistan.
CPEC, a major component of China's Belt and Road Initiative, connects Kashgar in Xinjiang with Gwadar Port via Pakistan; India opposes it because parts pass through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

subtopics.title: Sino-Indian Border: States, UTs and Sectors
subtopics.summary: India shares a 3,488 km boundary with China along the Himalayan range, and this border runs through one Union Territory and four states. Ladakh has the longest border segment with China among all Indian states and UTs, while Arunachal Pradesh has the second longest. For management purposes the Line of Actual Control is divided into Eastern, Middle and Western sectors, each grouping specific states and UTs.
facts: India shares a 3,488 km border with China along the Himalayan range.
The border runs through 5 entities: 1 UT (Ladakh) and 4 states (Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh).
Ladakh shares the longest border segment with China among all Indian states and UTs.
Arunachal Pradesh has the 2nd longest border segment with China.
Himachal Pradesh borders China and forms part of the Middle Sector.
Uttarakhand borders China and Nepal, among other states.
Sikkim borders China, Nepal and Bhutan.
LAC sectors: Eastern (Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim), Middle (Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh), Western (Ladakh).
Panchsheel Agreement was signed by Nehru and Zhou Enlai, with both sides pledging to respect each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

subtopics.title: Disputed Lines and Flashpoints
subtopics.summary: The India-China boundary is disputed in two main areas: Aksai Chin in the west and Arunachal Pradesh in the east. Each side relies on different historical lines, and China rejects the McMahon Line that India recognises. The disputes have produced repeated clashes, from the 1962 war to the 2017 Doklam standoff and the 2020 Galwan Valley clash.
facts: India considers Aksai Chin part of Ladakh and relies on the Johnson Line; China administers it as part of Xinjiang Autonomous Region and relies on the MacDonald Line.
India recognises the McMahon Line, demarcated at the 1914 Simla Convention, as the legal boundary; China rejects it and claims Arunachal Pradesh as South Tibet.
China contends that Tibet was not a sovereign state and could not conclude treaties, which is its reason for rejecting the Shimla agreement.
The term Line of Actual Control was introduced by Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai in 1959.
The LAC came into practical existence after the 1962 Sino-Indian War.
PLA invaded India on 20 Oct 1962; China declared a unilateral ceasefire on 19 Nov 1962 but retained Aksai Chin.
1967 Nathu La conflict and 1975 Tulung La ambush, in which four Indian soldiers were killed.
2017 Doklam plateau standoff lasted 73 days after India sent troops to stop China building a road.
15 Jun 2020 Galwan Valley clash: at least 20 Indian soldiers killed, the most serious clash in 50 years.

subtopics.title: Border Management Mechanisms and Agreements
subtopics.summary: India and China manage the LAC through a layered set of mechanisms and agreements rather than a final settlement of the boundary. The 2003 Special Representatives process is the highest political-level channel for a settlement, while the 2012 Working Mechanism coordinates responses to LAC incidents. Agreements from 1993 to 2013 added rules on peace, military activity near the LAC and face-to-face encounters between troops.
facts: Special Representatives on Boundary Question (2003) is the highest political-level mechanism for a final political settlement of the 3,488 km dispute.
Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (2012) is a diplomatic and military channel for LAC incidents and has no mandate to settle the boundary.
Corps Commander-level meetings pursue tactical disengagement, de-escalation and buffer-zone arrangements during major standoffs.
Border Personnel Meeting Points are designated locations where local military commanders address ground-level friction.
1993 Agreement for Maintenance of Peace and Tranquillity along the LAC recognised the LAC; it was signed during PM Narasimha Rao's visit to China.
1996 Confidence-Building Measures agreement restricted military activities and use of weapons near the LAC; signed during Jiang Zemin's visit to India.
2005 CBM Protocol set procedures for face-to-face encounters between troops.
2013 Border Defence Cooperation Agreement strengthened communication and coordination between border forces.

topics.title: Map Projections: From Mercator to Equal Earth

subtopics.title: Why flat maps must distort
subtopics.summary: The Earth is an oblate spheroid, so its curved surface cannot be shown on a flat map without distortion. A projection converts the 3D surface into a 2D representation, and no single flat map keeps area, shape, distance and direction exact at once. Conformal, equal-area and equidistant projections each preserve one property, while compromise projections balance distortion across all four.
facts: Earth is an oblate spheroid rather than a perfect sphere.
The oblate shape is due to Earth's rotation and uneven distribution of mass.
A projection converts Earth's 3D curved surface into a 2D representation.
Some degree of distortion is inevitably introduced by any projection.
The four properties are area, shape, distance and direction.
Conformal projections preserve angles and local shapes (e.g. Mercator).
Equal-area projections preserve relative areas (e.g. Equal Earth).
Equidistant projections preserve distance.
Compromise projections balance distortions but preserve none of the properties exactly.
Navigation and direction use conformal projections.

subtopics.title: Mercator projection and its distortion
subtopics.summary: The Mercator projection was introduced in 1569 by Gerardus Mercator and was primarily designed to assist maritime navigation. It is a cylindrical and conformal projection, so it keeps local shapes and shows rhumb lines as straight lines. The cost is that landmasses far from the Equator look much larger than they are, and Africa appears similar in size to Greenland.
facts: Introduced in 1569 by Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish geographer and cartographer.
Type: cylindrical and conformal projection.
Primarily designed to assist maritime navigation.
Earth's surface is conceptually projected onto a cylinder around the globe, then unfolded flat.
Stretching of parallels is matched exactly with stretching of meridians, which preserves shapes.
Landmasses far from the Equator appear much larger than they are.
Africa appears similar in size to Greenland, though Greenland is in reality 14 times smaller.
Rhumb lines appear as straight lines, which makes the projection useful for navigation.
Does not preserve relative area.

subtopics.title: Equal Earth and the Correct the Map resolution
subtopics.summary: Equal Earth is an equal-area, pseudo-cylindrical world projection created in 2018 to show landmass sizes accurately without severe shape distortion. The UN General Assembly adopted a 'Correct the Map' resolution, led by Togo, that promotes equal-area projections to address Mercator distortions. The resolution is not binding, so whether governments and classrooms adopt the new map remains to be seen.
facts: Equal Earth is an equal-area, pseudo-cylindrical world map projection, created in 2018.
Designed to display the entire globe while preserving relative landmass sizes accurately.
Avoids the severe, aesthetically jarring shape distortions common in earlier equal-area maps such as Gall-Peters.
The UN General Assembly adopted the 'Correct the Map' resolution promoting equal-area map projections.
Togo led the resolution through Foreign Minister Robert Dussey, under the #CorrectTheMap campaign.
The resolution was supported by 164 countries, including India.
The United States voted against it and six countries abstained.
The African Union endorsed it in August 2025 and the Caribbean Community backed it too.
Correct the Map is run by two advocacy groups, Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa.
India backed the resolution while drawing a firm line on depiction of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh; UN resolutions are not binding.

subtopics.title: Other projections and mapping in India
subtopics.summary: Gall-Peters, first presented in 1855 and popularised in 1973, preserves area but stretches or squashes shapes, while Robinson (1963) and Winkel Tripel (1921) are compromise projections. Winkel Tripel replaced Robinson in National Geographic Society maps in 1998. In India, the Survey of India, established in 1767, verifies international borders on published maps, and the Criminal Law Amendment Act (1961) penalises maps that misrepresent India's borders.
facts: The Gall-Peters projection was first presented by Scottish clergyman James Gall in 1855.
Arno Peters popularised the Gall-Peters projection in 1973.
Gall-Peters preserves area accurately but makes landmasses look stretched or squashed.
The Robinson projection (1963) was devised by Arthur H. Robinson to balance size and shape.
Robinson is a compromise projection, with meridians curving gently towards the Poles.
The Winkel Tripel projection (1921) was created by German cartographer Oswald Winkel.
Winkel Tripel aims to reduce distortion across area, distance and direction.
In 1998, Winkel Tripel replaced Robinson in National Geographic Society maps, followed by schools, textbooks and the World Bank.
The Survey of India, established in 1767, verifies international borders on published maps.
Criminal Law Amendment Act (1961), Section 2, penalises publication and distribution of maps that question India's territorial integrity or misrepresent its borders.

subtopics.title: Constitutional Status and Powers of the ECI
subtopics.summary: The Election Commission of India is a permanent, independent constitutional body under Articles 324 to 329 (Part XV), established in 1950. It administers elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, the President and the Vice President, and has been a three-member body since 1993. Its powers are administrative, advisory and quasi-judicial, and the Supreme Court in Mohinder Singh Gill (1977) treated the case as a cornerstone for its plenary powers.
facts: Permanent, all-India, quasi-judicial and independent constitutional body
Constitutional basis: Articles 324-329 (Part XV)
Ensures free and fair elections for Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice President
Three members since 1993: one CEC and two ECs
Administrative power: defining constituencies, preparing voter lists, scheduling elections
Advisory power: advises the President and Governors, guides during emergencies
Quasi-judicial power: resolves disputes over party recognition, allocates election symbols
Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1977): cornerstone case on ECI's plenary powers under Article 324
Where laws are silent (Articles 327 and 328), ECI can act independently to safeguard free and fair elections
ECI can order a re-poll if the purity of the electoral process is compromised; judicial review usually comes after the election

subtopics.title: Appointment, Tenure and Removal of CEC and ECs
subtopics.summary: The CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 replaced the 1991 Act and provides for appointment by the President on the recommendation of a Selection Committee, following the Supreme Court's directive in Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India (2023). The CEC and ECs enjoy Supreme Court Judge-level salary and benefits. The CEC serves for six years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier, and is removed through the same process as a Supreme Court Judge.
facts: Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India (2023): five-judge bench directed appointment on the advice of a Selection Committee
Earlier, the President made appointments on the advice of the Prime Minister
The 2023 Act replaced the Election Commission Act of 1991 on conditions of service and transaction of business
Selection Committee: Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister, and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha
Search Committee, headed by the Minister of Law and Justice, proposes a panel of five names
Selection Committee can consider names beyond the shortlist and can function despite vacancies
Tenure: six years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier; not eligible for re-appointment
An EC appointed as CEC: combined term as EC and CEC must not exceed six years
CEC and ECs enjoy Supreme Court Judge-level salary and benefits

subtopics.title: Why Semiconductors Matter
subtopics.summary: Semiconductors are foundational to modern technology and are used in automobiles, healthcare, defence, aerospace, telecommunications and consumer electronics. Chips with billions of transistors power high-performance computing and artificial intelligence, within a global electronics industry valued at approximately USD 4.3 trillion. COVID-19 exposed the risks of concentrated global supply chains, which has pushed countries to build domestic capabilities.

quizzes.title: Houthi Movement Check
quizzes.passage: The Houthi movement is an armed group in Yemen that has grown into one of the most powerful forces in the country's long conflict. It began as an opposition movement during the rule of Ali Abdullah Saleh, who had governed North Yemen for many years. The movement's early history is closely tied to a series of wars in Saada, a northern region, which started after the group's founder was killed by Yemeni forces. The 2011 uprising in Yemen, part of the wider Arab Spring, forced Saleh to hand over power to a new leader. The new government then faced an economic crisis and security threats from militant groups, including an al-Qaeda branch that captured territory in parts of the south and east. The Houthis used this instability to expand their territory, moving into the capital and later into western Yemen. Their growth drew a military response from Saudi Arabia, which intervened to restore the internationally recognised government. Observers describe the conflict in very different terms depending on their sympathies, which makes a settlement hard to reach. Today the Houthis remain a central actor in the Yemeni civil war, and their control over key areas shapes regional politics and maritime security along the Red Sea.

quizzes.title: Peace Deals Recall
quizzes.passage: Yemen's civil war has moved through phases of fighting, negotiation and fragile truces. After the Houthis took over large parts of the north, a Saudi-led coalition joined the conflict to support the government that is recognised internationally. Years of fighting put the Red Sea ports under heavy pressure, and trade and public revenues were disrupted as a result. Fighting continued along the coast for several years, and civilians in the affected areas faced shortages and displacement. Negotiators from the warring parties then tried to find a way out of the fighting through a package of agreements. The Stockholm Agreement was one such deal, and it covered several issues, including the city of Hodeidah and its ports. Ceasefire terms for Hodeidah set out how armed forces would move away from the ports and how the ports would be run by local forces. The agreements were meant to reduce violence and open a path to a wider political settlement. Diplomats kept returning to the talks table, hoping that partial deals could be turned into lasting arrangements. Implementation, however, remained difficult because each side had strong backers and deep mistrust of the other.

quizzes.title: Indus Waters Treaty: MCQ practice
quizzes.passage: The Indus Waters Treaty is a bilateral agreement between India and Pakistan that governs how the waters of the Indus river system are shared. The treaty divides the rivers into two groups. One group is available to one country with broad rights, while the other group is mainly allocated to the other country, which keeps only limited uses such as domestic supply, some irrigation and power generation from run-of-river plants. The agreement also sets out a layered system for resolving disputes, which runs from bilateral discussion to more formal procedures. Recently, a tribunal based in The Hague held that India cannot suspend the treaty by placing it in abeyance, and that the treaty remains in force. India rejected the ruling. New Delhi says the tribunal was not properly formed and has no jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions, so it has neither recognised the tribunal nor taken part in its proceedings. The episode has renewed debate about how the treaty's dispute procedures should work, especially when both countries pursue parallel proceedings.

quizzes.title: Dispute mechanism: typed answers
quizzes.passage: The Indus Waters Treaty sets out a graded system for handling disagreements between India and Pakistan. A standing bilateral body is meant to handle questions through discussion and exchange of information. Where a disagreement is technical rather than legal, it can be passed to an independent expert whose appointment is arranged through an outside institution. Formal legal disputes are meant to reach a court of arbitration, which is constituted under a formal annex to the treaty and has a fixed number of members. Both countries have at times run proceedings along two tracks at the same time, which has raised concerns about conflicting outcomes. When one such track was paused and later resumed, the order of steps became a central point of argument. India holds that the treaty must be followed in sequence, so that a legal tribunal takes up a case only after the earlier steps are exhausted. Pakistan has pursued its own route through arbitration. Meanwhile, restrictions on construction at one hydroelectric project remain linked to the outcome of the expert's work and stay in force for a period after the expert issues its final decision. The dispute has shown how much depends on the procedural order laid down in the treaty.

quizzes.title: Cardiff Pact MCQ set
quizzes.passage: Political leaders from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland signed a Memorandum of Understanding in Cardiff, asserting the principle of self-determination and calling for constitutional changes within the United Kingdom. The move has renewed debate over the UK's devolution framework, under which power is transferred from the central government to subnational institutions while ultimate constitutional authority stays at the centre. Devolution in the UK is asymmetric, because the extent and nature of devolved powers differ among the territories. The pact is a political understanding rather than a legally binding treaty. It asks Westminster to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change, and it affirms each nation's right to hold independence referendums. The UK government has rejected demands for new independence referendums, saying such votes need appropriate constitutional and legal authority. In the 2016 Brexit referendum, Scotland and Northern Ireland both voted to remain in the EU, which fed into these debates. Scotland and Wales would seek EU membership as new states, while Northern Ireland would rejoin the EU through unification with the Republic of Ireland. The pact is seen as the most coordinated challenge to the UK's union structure since the Good Friday Agreement.

quizzes.title: Union history TITA set
quizzes.passage: The United Kingdom was built in stages, and its constituent nations joined it at different times. Wales was brought into the English legal and political system through an Act of Union passed in the sixteenth century. The English and Scottish parliaments were united in 1707, creating a single new state. Ireland joined later, when another Act of Union brought it into the United Kingdom. Most of Ireland became independent after an Anglo-Irish War, while six counties in the north remained within the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland now each have devolved institutions, but the extent of their powers differs. Scotland's Parliament and Wales's legislature were set up by separate Acts of Parliament, and Westminster retains ultimate constitutional authority over all of these arrangements. After Brexit, Northern Ireland came to share a land border with an EU member state. New checks were then introduced between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and these checks angered Unionists who believed they undermined Northern Ireland's position within the UK. This layered history explains why devolution differs across the nations, and why these tensions continue to shape political debate.

The law gives the executive branch several trade tools, including tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas and tariffs on goods of Russian origin. Because the list of relevant buyers can change over time, the law provides for a periodic review carried out by the trade representative. Countries that rely only lightly on Russian gas, and that are actively cutting their imports, may qualify for a special exception. The framework's effect is also conditional, since it may be affected if Russia meets certain conditions linked to peace in Ukraine and to the stance of the Ukrainian government. For India, the measure is especially relevant because the country remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude, so Indian policymakers must weigh energy security against trade relations with the United States. quizzes.title: Legal tools check
quizzes.passage: Trade measures linked to Russian energy purchases raise questions about how long they will last. A tariff that rests only on a decision by the executive can be challenged in court, and courts can strike down a wide trade regime built on such a decision. A measure that has been passed by the legislature and signed into federal law carries greater legal permanence. American trade policy also relies on older statutes that give the government tools to respond to foreign practices. One of these allows the trade representative to examine unfair conduct by other countries. Another permits restrictions on imports when they are seen as a risk to national security. The government has also used tariffs on certain imported metals, and it has applied tariffs connected with goods produced through forced labour. For a country like India, such instruments matter because they change the cost of exports and make trade talks more complicated. Officials and businesses often watch these tools closely because a single measure can affect many sectors at once. quizzes.title: Joint Commission: Practice MCQs
quizzes.passage: Pakistan and China have set up a Boundary Joint Commission to watch over how their border management arrangements are put into practice. The body is meant to help the two sides coordinate on the everyday business of a shared frontier, including joint surveys, the flow of trade across the boundary and ties between people on either side. Its roots lie in an earlier bilateral framework on managing the boundary, which laid the groundwork for the new institution. The arrangement has drawn a firm response from India, which maintains that the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are integral parts of the country. New Delhi has questioned the move and reaffirmed its own claims over the territory concerned. The dispute centres on the Shaksgam Valley, a mountainous stretch in the Karakoram region, which came under a boundary agreement signed in the 1960s. Routes and infrastructure that link Xinjiang with Pakistan add to the importance of the arrangement, because they strengthen connectivity in a sensitive part of the western Himalayas. India therefore reads the Commission as part of a wider pattern of China-Pakistan coordination close to its own northern frontiers. Any arrangement touching this area is examined closely by New Delhi, which has long held that the territory forms part of India.

quizzes.passage: The boundary between India and China has never been fully settled, and disagreements over it have produced a long chain of confrontations. Two stretches of the frontier sit at the heart of the dispute. One lies in the high region of Aksai Chin, which the two sides understand differently, each relying on its own historical line. The other involves Arunachal Pradesh, which China describes as part of Tibet while India administers it as a full state. The line in that area was agreed at a convention attended by Tibet, China and British India, but China refused to accept it, arguing that Tibet could not conclude treaties. Armed encounters and standoffs have since erupted in several places, including mountain passes in Sikkim and Arunachal and the plateau where three countries meet. A practical dividing line emerged after the war of the early 1960s, and both sides have since tried to prevent escalation through talks and confidence-building measures. Local commanders meet at designated points to resolve friction on the ground, while senior commanders negotiate withdrawals when standoffs become serious. Yet incidents continue in the high mountains, and each new clash is watched closely by both capitals and by the wider region. Understanding these disputed lines is therefore essential for reading news about the border, since each claim carries a long history behind it.

quizzes.title: Properties of map projections
quizzes.passage: Every world map is an attempt to show a curved surface on a flat sheet, and that task cannot be done without some loss. The Earth is not a perfect sphere, and its surface is curved in every direction. Cartographers therefore use map projections, which are systematic rules for transferring the globe onto a plane. No single flat map can keep every feature of the globe correct at the same time. Mapmakers must choose which properties to protect, such as the size of landmasses, the shapes of countries, the distances between places, or the directions between them. Some maps are made to guide travellers at sea, while others help students compare the sizes of continents. A projection that works well for one purpose may mislead when used for another. Over time, different projections have been developed, each built around a different choice of property. Readers should therefore check which property a map keeps accurate before drawing conclusions about the world from its outlines. The choice of projection is a practical decision rather than a search for one perfect map. Understanding these trade-offs helps students read maps with care, and this is why many different projections continue to exist side by side in atlases, classrooms and official publications.

quizzes.title: Equal Earth and the Correct the Map campaign
quizzes.passage: A world map has to make choices, and the projection behind it decides which features look accurate. Many wall maps have long used a projection that suits navigation but makes landmasses far from the Equator look larger than they really are. Equal Earth is a newer world projection designed to display the entire globe while keeping the relative sizes of landmasses accurate. It avoids the severe, jarring shape distortions found in earlier equal-area maps. A campaign called Correct the Map has urged the wider use of equal-area projections, and two advocacy groups run it. Regional bodies have endorsed the idea, and the matter was taken up by the United Nations General Assembly. The resolution received wide support, but it also drew opposition and abstentions in the vote. Such a resolution carries political weight, yet it does not have binding force. Schools, publishers and governments are therefore free to decide whether to change the maps they use. Maps shape how people picture the size and position of countries. Choosing a projection is therefore a practical decision that depends on the purpose of the map. Readers should check what a map is designed to show before drawing conclusions from it. Only time will show whether the new map becomes common in classrooms and official documents.

quizzes.title: CEC Appointment and Removal: MCQ Set
quizzes.passage: The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body, placed under Part XV of the Constitution, that administers elections to Parliament, the State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice President. Its job is to ensure free and fair elections across the country. Since 1993, it has functioned as a three-member body, with one Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and two Election Commissioners (ECs). Earlier, the President made these appointments on the advice of the Prime Minister. In Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India (2023), a five-judge bench directed that the CEC and ECs be appointed on the advice of a Selection Committee. Parliament then passed the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 to comply with that directive. Under the Act, the Selection Committee consists of the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. A Search Committee, headed by the Minister of Law and Justice, prepares a panel of names for the Selection Committee to consider. The Opposition has recently announced plans to move a motion in Parliament seeking the removal of the CEC. This has drawn fresh attention to the constitutional safeguards that govern the independence and removal of the CEC.

quizzes.title: Electoral Rolls and SIR: Typed Answer Set
quizzes.passage: An electoral roll is the official list of individuals eligible to vote in a given election within a specific jurisdiction, and being listed on it is a legal prerequisite for casting a vote in India. The publishing and updating of electoral rolls are the joint responsibility of the Election Commission of India, the state's Chief Electoral Officer and the state's election commission. The Commission has broad authority over voter list management, and no individual may be excluded from electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex. The Commission can direct a fresh revision of rolls, which may be intensive, summary or a combination of both. An intensive revision involves a complete and fresh preparation of rolls through house-to-house enumeration, and it is done when the rolls are outdated, inaccurate or need complete rebuilding. A summary revision is a routine annual updating of existing rolls, while a special revision is undertaken in exceptional cases. The Special Intensive Revision is a focused, time-bound house-to-house verification of voters by Booth Level Officers, aimed at adding missing voters, removing ineligible ones and correcting entries. Such a revision excludes non-citizens and includes citizens aged 18 or above who are ordinarily resident in the constituency. Courts have also held that names cannot be removed from voter lists merely on suspicion, and the right to vote is treated as a statutory right rather than a fundamental one.

quizzes.title: Programme 2.0 and Its Pillars
quizzes.passage: Semiconductors have become central to modern life because they power automobiles, hospitals, defence systems, aircraft, telecom networks and a wide range of consumer goods. Modern chips can hold billions of transistors within very small areas, which makes them essential for high-performance computing, artificial intelligence and digital services. Semiconductors sit at the base of the global electronics industry, a very large economic sector. The COVID-19 pandemic showed how risky it is when chip production is concentrated in a few places, and many countries have since tried to build their own capabilities. India's response is a national programme that seeks to build a complete semiconductor ecosystem, covering design, fabrication, packaging, research and skilled manpower. The latest phase of this programme is a far larger policy framework than the original one. Its purpose is to give the sector financial and infrastructure support, so that domestic companies can grow and compete. The government hopes this will make India a dependable partner in the global value chain, in line with the vision of self-reliance and manufacturing for the world. Several areas of the programme are meant to move forward together, so that progress in design, equipment, factories and people keeps pace with one another. This approach turns a broad national goal into a set of concrete steps that can be tracked over time.

quizzes.title: Schemes and Partnerships in Brief
quizzes.passage: India's push into semiconductors uses several kinds of government support rather than a single measure. Some tools are aimed at manufacturing, with financial incentives for companies that set up production within the country and attract large investments. Others are aimed at design, because a country that can design its own chips depends less on imported technology. Academic institutions and start-ups are part of this effort, as they need access to specialised resources, training facilities and design infrastructure. Research bodies are also building their own processors, including designs based on an open instruction architecture, which adds to domestic technical strength. Support for design firms is planned over a long stretch so that they can move from early development to full deployment. Diplomacy plays a role as well. India has signed a strategic technology agreement with a major economy to expand cooperation in research, business and defence industry. It has also joined a coalition of countries that wish to protect the supply of critical minerals, manufacturing capacity and digital infrastructure. Together these steps reflect an attempt to lower dependence on other countries and to become a dependable part of the global chip supply network, which matters greatly in a world where supply disruptions can hurt many industries at once.

quizzes.title: Framework and rules check
quizzes.passage: The Unified Payments Interface has grown into a large digital payment network that handles billions of transactions every month. Running such a network requires continuous spending on technology, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, server capacity and customer support. Until now, merchants have not paid any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions, which helped small businesses and informal sectors adopt digital payments. As the network expands, however, planners must decide how its upkeep should be funded. The answer proposed in the new framework is a fee on certain merchant payments, while everyday low-value transactions remain free. Officials have stressed that small merchants and ordinary users should not face additional costs. The fee is therefore aimed at larger merchant payments rather than at the many small transactions that make up daily life. Such a structure lets the payment ecosystem generate revenue that supports its own operation. Policymakers have sought a balance between funding the network and protecting the people who use it every day. UPI works in real time and around the clock, connecting individuals and merchants across banks. Its wide use has made it an important part of commerce, from neighbourhood shops to large retailers. Because so many people rely on it, any change to how the network is priced affects a very large number of users and businesses.

quizzes.title: Exemptions and caps check
quizzes.passage: Digital payments work best when small transactions stay cheap for everyone who uses them. Households send money to one another every day, and shopkeepers in local markets often accept payments through a QR code displayed at the counter. Many of these businesses operate on thin margins, so an extra charge on each small sale can matter a great deal. Policymakers have therefore tried to protect the smallest users while still asking larger participants to share the cost of running the network. The new approach separates payments into groups. Some payments remain free regardless of who sends or receives them, while others attract a charge only when they are large. Certain sectors that provide essential services are placed in a separate group, where a fixed charge per transaction applies rather than a percentage. Investments routed through mutual funds and securities are charged at a lower rate, because that rate is meant to encourage greater use of digital payments in formal financial markets. Several upper limits also protect users. A single ceiling prevents very large payments from carrying an unlimited fee, and small merchants who earn only modest amounts through QR codes each month are exempt from the charge altogether. Together, these rules aim to keep ordinary digital payments affordable while the payment infrastructure keeps growing.

quizzes.passage: Financial and trade cooperation was among the most detailed areas of the 18th BRICS Summit, which India hosted in New Delhi in 2026. Small enterprises received particular attention, since many of them need steady cash flow to run their operations and compete in international markets. Support for young companies also formed part of the discussions. On the tax and customs side, the summit focused on sharing knowledge between national tax authorities and on joint action against smuggling and illicit financial flows, while stressing that genuine trade should continue without unnecessary obstruction. Officials framed these discussions as part of a broader effort to make economic relationships more balanced and predictable, especially for countries that rely heavily on trade with partners outside their immediate regions. Culinary exchanges were also part of the summit, with regional produce showcased to delegates. Officials said these measures were designed to work alongside existing mechanisms rather than replace them. quizzes.title: SCO origins: typed answers

quizzes.title: UNGA, P4M and India's Stand

The initiative was conceived in response to the erosion of global consensus, trade weaponisation and escalating conflicts across Europe and West Asia. It was conceptualised by leaders of the European Union, Brazil, Kenya and Canada, and is co-sponsored by India, Australia and Barbados. It is designed as an open and flexible framework rather than another exclusive international bloc or permanent bureaucracy. It seeks to strengthen international law, peace, multilateral cooperation and inclusive prosperity, and to enable countries from different political traditions to cooperate on reforming multilateral institutions and addressing common global challenges. quizzes.title: Reading the Index
quizzes.passage: Gender equality is often discussed in terms of laws and policies, but measuring it is a separate challenge. One widely cited tool is the Global Gender Gap Index, which is published every year as a flagship report. Its purpose is not simply to count how many women hold particular positions. Instead, it asks how far each country has moved toward closing the disparities between women and men. This focus on gaps rather than absolute outcomes shapes the whole report. Each country receives a numerical score, and these scores allow nations to be compared on a common yardstick. One end of the range signals complete equality, while the other end signals absolute inequality. The scores can also be presented on a more familiar scale, where the highest value stands for full parity. Because the report is repeated each year, observers can see whether countries are moving forward or falling behind. Readers should remember that a ranking captures relative progress among the countries covered. It does not, by itself, describe the daily experience of women in any single society. Understanding the method behind the scores is therefore as important as reading the final table.

quizzes.title: NCAP numbers check
quizzes.passage: The National Clean Air Programme is a national-level strategy launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change to address air pollution through coordinated interventions across sectors. The National Air Quality Index is a tool for communicating air quality status to people in terms that are easy to understand. quizzes.title: NISAR radar check

Conventional cameras depend on visible light, but radar works differently. A synthetic aperture radar sends microwave pulses toward the ground and builds images from the returning signals, so it can produce sharp pictures in darkness and through clouds. The satellite is meant to study changes in the solid Earth. Its images help track surface deformation, which is useful for understanding earthquakes, volcanic activity and landslides. The same data can also support monitoring of floods, biomass, deforestation, crop health and soil moisture. The booklet calls its radar technology among the finest synthetic aperture radar systems ever designed. Its large receiving antenna and wide imaging swath make it suitable for mapping large surface areas in three dimensions. Because the satellite can detect minute ground shifts, its data is used for tectonic and structural analysis, and repeated observations of the same areas help show how the ground changes over time.

Match List I with List II:

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

quizzes.title: Economy and Schemes: Key Numbers
quizzes.passage:
Several economic and infrastructure stories were in the news this month. The Union Cabinet approved a scheme to promote new surface coal and lignite gasification projects that produce syngas, building on the National Coal Gasification Mission launched in 2021. Gasification converts coal into a gaseous fuel instead of burning it directly, and the scheme is part of a wider national objective for coal gasification capacity by 2030. Eligible projects receive financial assistance on their plant and machinery, subject to ceilings for each project, each product and each entity.

In electric mobility, NITI Aayog and World Resources Institute India released the India Electric Mobility Index 2025. It evaluates how States and Union Territories are progressing towards electric mobility on a scale of 0 to 100, using three pillars: transport electrification progress, charging infrastructure readiness and EV research and innovation. Delhi retained the highest overall position.

A long-pending inter-state project, the Kishau Multipurpose Dam, has also moved forward. It is planned on the Tons River, a tributary of the Yamuna, and several States and Union Territories have reached agreement on its implementation.

Urban statistics were discussed too. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs told a Parliamentary panel that the criteria for identifying a Census Town may no longer reflect India's changing urbanisation. A Census Town is treated as urban for Census purposes even though it may not be a formally notified urban local body.

Finally, India's foreign exchange reserves reached a record high, a rise linked mainly to inflows through RBI's concessional swap arrangements tied to FCNR(B) deposits.

questions.q: What percentage of the cost of the water component will the Union Government provide as Central Assistance for the Kishau Multipurpose Dam Project? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The Union Government provides 90% of the cost of the water component, and the remaining 10% is shared by the participating States/UT.

questions.q: Up to what percentage of expenditure on plant and machinery will the government provide as financial assistance under the new coal and lignite gasification scheme? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the government will provide financial assistance of up to 20% of expenditure on plant and machinery.

questions.q: How many performance indicators does the India Electric Mobility Index 2025 use to evaluate States and Union Territories?
questions.explanation: The index is evaluated on a 0-100 scale across 16 performance indicators.

questions.q: How many States/UTs are participating in the Kishau Multipurpose Dam Project?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists six participating States/UT: Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan.

questions.q: What minimum population must a settlement have to qualify as a Census Town under the criteria introduced for the 1981 Census? (in persons)
questions.explanation: A Census Town must have at least 5,000 persons, along with an occupational and a population density condition.

questions.q: After the recent rise, what global rank did India attain in foreign exchange reserves? (ordinal)
questions.explanation: India moved to 4th position globally, ahead of Russia and after China, Japan and Switzerland.

questions.q: What weight, in per cent, does the Transport Electrification Progress pillar carry in the India Electric Mobility Index 2025? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The transport electrification pillar carries 50% of the index, with charging infrastructure at 30% and EV research and innovation at 20%.

quizzes.title: Blue Bonds and the Navier-Stokes Claim
quizzes.passage:
Financial markets are looking beyond conventional projects towards the health of the seas and rivers. A new category of debt instrument is emerging to pay for work that keeps marine and freshwater ecosystems usable and protected over the long term. India plans to join this market through a bond issued by a company that focuses on the maritime sector. The bond will be arranged by a bank's capital markets arm, which has been appointed as arranger. Governments elsewhere have already experimented with similar tools, so the idea is not entirely new.

Science also produced a headline this month. A technology company said that an advanced artificial intelligence model had produced a proposed solution to a long-standing puzzle about how fluids move. Such claims are checked with formal tools that test every step of an argument. The puzzle concerns the equations that describe the motion of water, air and honey, and it belongs to a small group of famous challenges that a mathematics institute has highlighted.

Those equations are not merely theoretical. Engineers rely on them when they design aircraft and automobiles, and scientists use them to predict weather and model currents in the ocean. Progress on the puzzle would therefore matter far beyond mathematics, and that is why the claim has drawn wide attention.

questions.q: India's proposed blue bond is best described as a sub-category of which broader instrument?
questions.explanation: The booklet describes the blue bond as a thematic sub-category of green bonds.

questions.q: In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute designated the Navier-Stokes problem as one of how many Millennium Prize Problems?
questions.explanation: The booklet states the Clay Mathematics Institute designated seven Millennium Prize Problems in 2000.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:
A. Sagarmala Finance Corporation Limited is India's first maritime sector-specific NBFC.
B. Ocean-current modelling is one of the applications of the fluid equations.
C. The Navier-Stokes problem was designated a Millennium Prize Problem in 2010.
D. Seychelles issued the world's first sovereign blue bond in 2019.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements A and B are in the booklet, while C (2010) and D (2019) contradict the booklet's dates.

questions.q: The OpenAI proof claim was reportedly checked using Lean. In the booklet, Lean is described as what?
questions.explanation: The booklet describes Lean as a computer-based proof assistant designed to check mathematical arguments step by step.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Navier-Stokes problem:
I. The fluid equations are based on conservation of mass and Newton's second law of motion.
II. The Clay Mathematics Institute designated this problem in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems.
III. The fluid equations describe the motion of water and honey, but not air.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement III is false because the booklet says the fluid equations describe air as well as water and honey.

questions.q: Which country implemented a Debt-for-Ocean Swap in 2021 to support marine conservation?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that Belize implemented a Debt-for-Ocean Swap in 2021 to support marine conservation.

quizzes.title: Schemes, Events and Honours
quizzes.passage:
September brought a mix of schemes, events and honours. The country marked International Literacy Day with a national festival that focused on adults who never learned to read. The programme is meant to build basic reading, writing and calculating skills among learners who have passed the age of school, so that they can take part fully in public life.

Water also featured in the news. A major conference on water management brought together experts, officials and delegates to discuss solutions that can withstand a changing climate. The event is a flagship initiative of a central government ministry, and it has been rebranded for the current year.

In cinema, the nation's highest honour is named after a pioneer of Indian films. The award recognises an individual's outstanding contribution to the growth and development of Indian cinema. This year's recipient is a veteran actor from Karnataka, and he follows an earlier recipient from the same regional film industry.

Beauty pageants made headlines too. The Miss World contest crowned a new titleholder from the Dominican Republic at its latest edition, and the next edition has already been planned for a future year in another country. An Indian contestant secured a place among the top forty.

questions.q: In which year was the Dadasaheb Phalke Award instituted?
questions.explanation: The booklet gives the year of institution of the award as 1969.

questions.q: In which year was Raja Harishchandra, directed by the award's namesake and regarded as India's first full-length feature film, made?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that Dadasaheb Phalke directed Raja Harishchandra in 1913.

questions.q: In which city did the ULLAS Mela mark the conclusion of the International Literacy Day 2026 celebrations?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the 2026 celebrations concluded with the ULLAS Mela in New Delhi.

questions.q: In which year was India Water Week first conceptualised, before its 2026 rebranding? (year)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that India Water Week was conceptualised in 2012.

questions.q: In which financial year does the implementation period of the ULLAS scheme end? (financial year)
questions.explanation: The booklet says ULLAS is implemented during 2022-23 to 2026-27.

questions.q: In which Vietnamese city was the 73rd edition of Miss World held?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the 73rd edition of Miss World was held in Nha Trang, Vietnam.

questions.q: Which country will host the next Miss World edition, scheduled for 2027?
questions.explanation: The booklet notes that the next Miss World edition is scheduled to be hosted in Tanzania in 2027.
